speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I thought it would be useful for me to first share the history and context in which it was first introduced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When Singapore was still under British rule, the Raffles Town Plan, also known as the Jackson Plan, designated separate geographical zones for each ethnic group.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Malays, Chinese, Indians and Europeans lived in different areas and apart from one another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But this segregation was not conducive to promoting interaction and integration between the races.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Given the experience as well as the circumstances that led to Singapore’s Independence in 1965, our founding fathers were determined to learn these lessons in order to build a cohesive, multiracial society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our very existence as a nation was based on this ideal: that we would be one united people, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: To achieve this aspiration, the Government did not blindly paper over the differences between the ethnic groups.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We also did not take a "melting-pot" approach by forcing the different races to blend or conform artificially to one uniform national culture.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Instead, we respected and celebrated our differences, worked hard to uplift every community while actively enlarging our common space, and fostering trust and understanding between the various ethnic communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We encouraged this through a range of policies, including public housing policy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, when the Housing and Development Board (HDB) built new towns and estates to provide public housing for Singaporeans, we consciously allocated flats in such a way that every HDB block and precinct all over Singapore reflected the ethnic mix of the general population.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This was so that people of different races could interact and form bonds with one another.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While we controlled the allocation of new flats quite carefully, we did not initially place similar restrictions on resale transactions, which were first allowed in 1971.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over time, as more resale transactions took place, people sold and bought and moved, ethnic concentrations started to re-emerge in particular areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, by the late 1980s, we started to observe an increasing concentration of Chinese buyers in Ang Mo Kio and Malay buyers in Bedok and Tampines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It caps the proportion of flats in each HDB block and neighbourhood that can be owned by households of each ethnic group.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The limits are set based on the ethnic proportions in the general population, with an allowance for some local variations in each block and neighbourhood.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if you look at the EIP limits, they are actually set higher than the national demographic proportion of each ethnic group.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong pointed out the changing profile of our households.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We, therefore, review the EIP limits regularly, to ensure that they are in line with national demographics so that our HDB blocks and neighbourhoods continue to reflect the multiracial character of our society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: As for inter-ethnic households, which are becoming increasingly common in our social landscape, they can choose which ethnic quota to be considered when buying a flat.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This choice is then fixed until they sell the flat, to be fair to other flat owners.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Today, we have made progress in strengthening good relations among Singaporeans of all races.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is the result of the hard work put in by many generations of Singaporeans, as well as our deliberate policies and programmes that seek to actively support multiracialism, including the EIP.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But as recent incidents show, there is still more that we can and must do to combat racism.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Building racial harmony is a constant work in progress.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The EIP remains an important part of this effort because, left entirely to social and market forces, ethnic concentrations will start forming in different areas again.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There are many reasons for this, even beyond instinctive preferences that people may have, to live near others from the same ethnic community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For example, family members may wish to live near each other for mutual support, that is, live near family.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or residents of certain ethnic groups may prefer neighbourhoods with a higher concentration of specific amenities and services or larger flat types.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Or they may find different locations more suitable for their household’s financial situation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Individually, these are completely understandable and reasonable preferences and very personal ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But collectively, if we are not careful, these tendencies could, inadvertently, lead to segregation among our races.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This happens across all ethnic groups – Chinese, Malays, Indians and Others – as well as in both mature estates with older Singaporeans and newer estates with younger residents, where most residents fulfilled the Minimum Occupation Period in recent years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, just imagine how much more the different ethnic groups would concentrate in different neighbourhoods, if we did away with the EIP, and how much harder it would be then to promote mixing and understanding across ethnic groups in the home environment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Our children could grow up in neighbourhoods where they hardly see any children or any people of other races, not even in their classrooms, since most children go to pre-schools and national schools near their homes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: How much harder then would it be for them to even get acquainted with different cultures from a young age – to see festivities, celebrations and mourning in the neighbourhood – not to mention to truly understand and appreciate these cultures from a very young age?

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Of course, some might argue that just because we live next door to someone from a different ethnic group, culture or religion, it does not necessarily mean that we will get along with our neighbour, or learn to tolerate or understand our differences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, all these incidents of friction between neighbours of different cultures have caught our attention and is part of the reason why are having this debate today.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But equally, often, we do not celebrate the large number of situations when neighbours learn to live with each other, celebrate each other's festivals, mourn with each other, grieve with each other and go and learn how to live together, because they live in the same community.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With diversity in our estates, we get to interact with our neighbours of different races almost every day – along the corridors, the void decks, playgrounds, markets, neighbourhood centres, shops, hawker centres.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And if we do not live with one another, it makes it much harder to empathise with other communities and understand the challenges that they face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And so much easier to stereotype or assume the worst of the other, the people we do not see or do not see so often.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And this is a recipe for mutual mistrust and intolerance that we have seen in our early history but also repeated in cities and townships all around the world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Indeed, we only need to look at other countries in the present day to see how this might happen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In major cities across Europe and the United States (US), for example, racial segregation is common and well-advanced.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The wealthier ethnicities congregate in expensive, gentrified precincts.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: While ethnicities which are less well-off are excluded and stigmatised.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They receive fewer opportunities and these differences get entrenched across generations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: I recently read an article on the website FiveThirtyEight analysing racial segregation in the US.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It featured a tool developed by the University of Virginia which is called "The Racial Dot Map" – and you might want to check it up after this.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The map plots one dot for each person on the maps of US cities, with different colours representing different ethnicities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The map is colourful, but you can see distinct and clear patches of colour sharply separated from one another, with very little inter-mixing, a reflection of how multicultural but segregated the country is.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The author also cites a study showing that three quarters of white Americans do not have any non-white friends.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He writes, I quote, "The places we live affect not only our access to resources, but also who we meet, interact with and become friends with.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The nature of segregation in the US means that we only end up seeing and learning about what our own groups experience, making it hard to understand the lives of people outside of our own group."  Similarly, after I spoke about the EIP at an overseas conference some years back, a mayor of a big city that suffered from serious racial segregation and conflict came up to me.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: He said he wished that his city had implemented a version of the EIP much earlier on, to foster harmony and avert the unrest that they now regularly face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But now that societal divisions have hardened along racial and ethnic lines, the EIP is not a feasible nor politically attainable option.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Even talking about the idea of ensuring that different races live near one another would cause an uproar and inflame tensions even further.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is how bad the situation had become.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That conversation with this mayor has stuck in my mind all these years.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In fact, in September 2016, Lord Mayor Sadiq Khan of London, said this: "The less integrated our societies are, the greater the economic and social costs we face now and in the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Failure to integrate feeds extremism, whether in the Muslim community or the far right.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It causes anxiety and fear of crime and causes mistrust between people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A laissez-faire approach to achieving social integration just does not work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: There is so much that city leaders can do to ensure people of different ethnicities, faiths, culture, age groups and incomes do not just tolerate each other, but live truly interconnected lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We need to ensure that our housing and planning laws mean we design and build integrated communities and institutions where neighbours have real reasons to come together." And, actually, I have got many other studies that we have been following over the years – studies in Europe, the US and other cities – which affirm that integration and social diversity strengthen social cohesion and understanding.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, the EIP continues to serve a very important function for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We cannot leave social mixing to chance and hope that it will happen by an invisible hand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: It is better to intervene upstream to pre-empt the problem and to foster mutual understanding and encourage integration from the start.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: If we wait until after racial tensions have started to bubble to the surface and develop and become entrenched, it will become so much harder to heal those fractures and rebuild trust among different communities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: From our engagements and the feedback we have received, most Singaporeans understand and support the EIP and recognise its purpose.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Similar levels of support were seen across all races.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: About 30% were indifferent to this and less than 10% disagreed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Having said that, we recognise that the EIP is an intrusive social policy, because it acts against very powerful and complex socio-economic forces that are at play in Singapore and all over the world.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And in its application on the ground, the EIP does have its rough edges and may cause difficulties for some owners looking to sell their flats.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: When the EIP limits are reached for an ethnic group, sellers from other ethnic groups are unable to sell to buyers of the constrained group.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: With a smaller pool of eligible buyers, sellers may have to lower their asking price or they may take longer to market and sell their flat.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This happens across all races, including Chinese sellers who are affected by the non-Chinese EIP limits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But we do see more appeals from sellers from the minority races.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is because Chinese buyers form a larger proportion of the market simply from the demographic mix of society and the impact on individual non-Chinese sellers is therefore larger when the Chinese EIP limits are reached.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: And this data we presented in some Parliamentary Questions (PQs) earlier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: In such cases, the seller’s loss may be the buyer’s gain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: A buyer from an eligible race will benefit from a lower resale price and would thus be less affected if and when they sell the flat in the future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But this brings little comfort to affected sellers, particularly those who had bought the flat from HDB, or on the resale market before the EIP limits were reached, and yet are now caught by the EIP limits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is the group who can be financially disadvantaged, and I understand why they feel aggrieved.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: They may feel it is unfair that they are personally shouldering the costs for a policy that benefits all of us in society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: Over the years, Members of Parliament on both sides of this House have raised these concerns.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: This is why HDB has been exercising flexibility for EIP-constrained owners, on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: For instance, HDB will give the household more time to sell their flat and even waive the EIP limits if there are exceptional circumstances.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: However, whenever HDB waives EIP limits to address its impact on certain households, it is mindful that this may lead to even higher imbalances in the concentrations of certain ethnic groups in some areas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, we are studying the situation carefully and are looking at what more can be done to help affected sellers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: The EIP is by no means the perfect tool, nor the only tool to promote and ensure racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We are very conscious of the trade-offs and will keep working to smoothen its sharper edges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: But it has an essential place among the range of tools, programmes, policies and safeguards we deploy to protect and promote our racial harmony.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: So, let us keep in mind the larger social objective behind the EIP even as we seek to smoothen its sharper edges.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: We must always ensure that the places we live and grow up reflect the fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Desmond Lee
text: That is how we continuously press on towards our ideal of a cohesive and multi-racial Singapore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We are taking PQs all the way to Question No 16.
